There are also unconfirmed reports that opposition from European policymakers, including concerns about stablecoins and their impact on the digital euro, may have played a role in the rejection.

📌 Token Vesting: Why Team and Investor Tokens Unlock Over Time

Main Points
⏺ Token vesting schedules control when founders, teams, and investors can claim their tokens
⏺ Unlocks are usually spread over months or years with cliffs and linear releases
⏺ This post explains how vesting protects projects from instant dump pressure

1️⃣ What Is Vesting — tokens reserved for insiders are locked and only become claimable at set dates
2️⃣ Cliff Period — an initial lockup (for example, 6–12 months) where no tokens unlock at all
3️⃣ Linear Unlock — after the cliff, tokens are released gradually, such as monthly over several years
4️⃣ Market Impact — large unlocks can increase sell pressure, so traders often track vesting calendars
5️⃣ Trust Signal — transparent vesting shows that core contributors are aligned for the long term, not just a quick exit

Final Thoughts

Token vesting turns insider allocations into a time-based commitment — the longer they’re locked in, the more skin in the game the project really has.

The bigger issue is funding. After spending much of its ETH reserves on ecosystem growth, EF plans to cut annual spending from 15% to 5% by 2030. Meanwhile, its 4-year Client Incentive Program ended in April 2026 with no replacement announced.

Maintaining client teams, research, and protocol coordination costs around $30M per year. Without a sustainable funding model, Ethereum risks losing experienced developers and slowing progress on scaling, quantum-resistance research, and core network maintenance.

Ethereum’s biggest challenge may not be technology—it may be funding the people building it.

Nuclear Theater: Inspectors, Illusions, and Enriched Ego

Rafael Grossi flies to Fukushima and does what technocrats do: waves a memorandum and says the rules are clear. 

According to him, the U.S.–Iran understanding explicitly puts all nuclear activity and material under IAEA supervision, “in all letters,” which means inspectors will enter enrichment sites sooner or later. 

He talks like timing is a scheduling issue — tomorrow, a week, ten days — not a power struggle, and insists inspections are “going to happen” because the paper says so.

Tehran answers with a cold shrug. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi says access to bombed sites and to the high‑grade uranium will “only” be reviewed within a final deal and only after sanctions are actually lifted, not just promised on TV. 

He denies any cozy side‑meeting with Grossi in Switzerland, and warns against people trying to “stir up and take over” reality through media hype — his polite way of saying Vienna and Washington are gaslighting the world with press conferences instead of binding commitments.

Trump, meanwhile, does his own version of nuclear improv on Fox. He tells viewers there’s “no rush” to let inspectors in, and that American teams will walk in alongside IAEA staff “to find the enriched uranium,” like it’s an Easter egg hunt with satellite imagery and airstrikes as the clues. Just weeks earlier he was boasting that any remaining enriched uranium would be handed over to the U.S. or “destroyed in place” under American supervision — which sounds tough until you remember Grossi keeps saying the IAEA still can’t verify where the bulk of that material actually is.

So you get three realities for the price of one. The IAEA insists the framework deal obliges Iran to open the doors and that it’s just a matter of logistics. Iran insists nothing happens until the last sanction is gone and every access request is folded into a final, face‑saving agreement. 

Trump insists the uranium is already under control, or soon will be, as long as he’s in the room when the cameras roll. Nobody can actually verify the status of the stockpile since the June strikes, but everyone sells certainty to their own public: Grossi sells “oversight,” Tehran sells “sovereignty,” Trump sells “victory.”

From a distance, it looks less like arms control and more like narrative control. The watchdog needs to prove it matters, so it declares inspections inevitable. The regime needs to prove it didn’t cave, so it delays any access to the sites that really count. The U.S. president needs to prove he “solved” Iran, so he downplays the risk of near‑bomb‑grade uranium buried in tunnels while promising American inspectors will personally babysit it. 

And between all these performances sits the actual material that could make up to ten nuclear weapons, unvisited, unverifiable, and far more stable than the politicians arguing over it.

❗️ According to posts shared by CoinMarketCap and crypto-focused accounts on X, Ripple expects to end 2026 with a $1 billion revenue run rate. The figure does not include XRP held on Ripple’s balance sheet. That detail matters because Ripple has long faced public debate over the link between its business and XRP. Garlinghouse’s target frames the company as a fintech infrastructure provider that aims to earn money from products, clients, and services, not from token holdings or sales.

🌐 The deal also supports Ripple USD, known as RLUSD. Ripple has promoted the stablecoin for enterprise settlement and collateral use. Recently, crypto news reported that Ripple is also adding RLUSD to new payment tools, including services tied to AI agents and machine payments on the XRP Ledger. Company materials point to custody, treasury management, and liquidity services as core offerings. These products target banks and firms that need faster settlement, account control, and access to digital assets through regulated processes, rather than retail trading.
